extracted.intended_audience: tourists and general travellers planning a trip to Edinburgh
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, on-the-ground advice for travellers visiting Edinburgh covering when to go, what to pack, transport, etiquette, safety and accessibility. The list gives actionable tips for planning a short city break or longer stay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arriving in Edinburgh
rubrics_metrics.description: Edinburgh's airport is 8 miles (13km) away. Buses (cheaper), trams (quicker when the roads are busy) and taxis (good for door-to-door drop-offs) connect the terminal with the city center. Train passengers roll into Edinburgh Waverley; buses arrive at St Andrew’s Square in the New Town.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose transport by cost vs speed: bus for cheaper transfer, tram for quicker journeys during traffic, taxi for door-to-door convenience. If arriving by train from England expect scenic coastal views. Note central drop-off/arrival points (Waverley, St Andrew’s Square).

rubrics_metrics.name: When to visit — come in summer for a chance of sunshine
rubrics_metrics.description: Summer has long, bright days and generally docile winds and will suit most visitors best. If you don’t mind 'dreich' (dismal) weather, colder months offer warm pubs and museums plus bracing strolls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick season based on weather tolerance and activities: summer for daylight and outdoor exploring; shoulder/winter months for cheaper travel, museums and pub culture. Expect quick weather changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the Festival unless you’re attending
rubrics_metrics.description: The Edinburgh International Festival (and Fringe) takes over the city every August. If you’re going, book accommodation months in advance and book big shows early. If not attending, avoid August. Hogmanay (New Year run-up) is also very busy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan far ahead for August/Hogmanay—expect crowds, high prices and sold-out shows. If you want quieter city time, avoid peak festival dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pack waterproof gear
rubrics_metrics.description: You’ll need a jacket whenever you’re visiting. Edinburgh can change from bright sunshine to heavy rain quickly. You’ll likely be walking a lot, so comfortable shoes are important. No need to pack particularly formal wear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring a lightweight waterproof jacket and comfy walking shoes; layer for variable conditions. Leave formalwear at home unless you have a specific plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Booking in advance can be worth it
rubrics_metrics.description: Earlier booking of accommodation is better, especially during festival time. The Edinburgh City Pass is worth a look if visiting attractions (Castle, Royal Yacht Britannia) and includes city bus tours. Booking the castle online a day or so before can save money and waiting time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For popular shows (e.g., the Tattoo) or peak dates, book months ahead. Consider passes for bundled entry and skip-the-line savings. Use online prebook for attractions to reduce queues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the Old Town vs New Town
rubrics_metrics.description: Central Edinburgh is split by a valley containing Princes Street Gardens and Waverley Station. The Old Town is medieval with packed tenements, cobbled streets and wynds off the Royal Mile; the New Town (around 250 years old) has airy boulevards and an orderly grid. Other districts include the West End, Leith and the Southside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Old/New Town distinction for itinerary planning: Old Town for historic atmosphere and Royal Mile; New Town for Georgian architecture and easier navigation. Explore beyond center to West End and Leith for different vibes.

rubrics_metrics.name: How long to stay
rubrics_metrics.description: One day is enough for a whistle-stop tour of the Royal Mile and the castle; two days gives a sense of Old and New Towns; four days or more gives a proper feel including Leith and the Gallery of Modern Art and allows ticking off the big sights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose stay length based on depth desired: 1 day for highlights, 2 days for a fuller city feel, 4+ days for side districts and museums. Build in walking time between areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Currency and payments
rubrics_metrics.description: Scotland has its own banknotes, but English notes are accepted everywhere in Scotland (some English shops may not accept Scottish notes). Card and contactless payments are now more common than cash; buses may require exact change if you pay cash, or use a pass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer card/contactless for convenience. If using cash on buses, have exact change or buy a pass. Be aware of Scottish vs English banknotes when carrying cash.

rubrics_metrics.name: LGBTQ+ scene: the Pink Triangle
rubrics_metrics.description: Edinburgh’s gay scene is centred on the 'Pink Triangle' just northeast of Princes Street. CC Blooms is a mainstay with daytime food and night cabaret/DJs; the Regent in Abbeyhill is a laid-back alternative. Same-sex marriage was legalised in Scotland in 2014.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Head to the Pink Triangle for LGBTQ+ nightlife and venues. Expect a mix of cabaret, DJs and daytime venues; check venue details for events and prices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Old Reekie — local nickname and history
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Old Reekie' dates from the 17th century when the Old Town’s narrow streets plus the Nor Loch produced a notorious smoke-and-effluent odour. Today the city smells much like any other, though parts of the West End can have a brewery-related boozy smell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is historical context rather than a current hygiene warning — expect normal urban smells with occasional local brewery aromas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Getting around — walking is best
rubrics_metrics.description: Edinburgh is hilly but walking is the best way to get around to pass views and feel the city’s rhythms. For longer trips across town, use a cab (Central Taxis) or ride-sharing app (Uber). Trams link the city centre and West End with the airport; buses help reach Leith or the Southside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wear comfortable shoes for walking; use cabs/ride-hailing for long cross-town trips or when tired. Note there is no subway.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't offend the locals — etiquette
rubrics_metrics.description: Informal 'hi' or a handshake are usual greetings. Avoid politics and religion in small talk; Scottish independence and Brexit can inspire passionate responses. Remember Edinburgh is in Scotland (part of Britain) but distinct from England — the England football team is often booed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep small talk neutral; be aware local sensitivities around national identity and politics. Use friendly, informal greetings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mind your tongue — local words and pronunciations
rubrics_metrics.description: Expect a range of accents and local words: haar (sea fog), Jambos (Hearts fans), Hibbies (Hibernian fans), Weegies (Glaswegians), salt ‘n sauce (condiment). Pronounce Cockburn Street as 'Coe-burn' and Edinburgh as 'Edin-bru' or 'Embra.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn a few local terms and correct pronunciations to help communication and avoid embarrassment. Be ready for unfamiliar slang and varying accents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pub culture — buy your round
rubrics_metrics.description: One person usually orders for the group at the bar, paying for the 'round' of drinks and bringing them back; everyone then takes turns to get the round. Some bars offer table service, and trays are often available. Most places accept card/phone payments but many still take cash. Pubs usually stay open until midnight or 1am.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow local custom by participating in rounds if invited. Check payment methods and opening hours; expect later closing times than in southern England.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tipping practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Tipping is mainly required for table service in restaurants (10–15%). Locals often round up taxi fares. Hotel porters typically get a tip of a pound or two per bag.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tip restaurant table service around 10–15% if service is good; round up taxis; give small per-bag amounts to porters. Do not feel obliged to tip in all situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety — generally safe but be cautious
rubrics_metrics.description: Edinburgh is relatively safe. Pub-packed areas get lively on weekends but serious trouble is rare. Calton Hill offers good day views but is best avoided at night. Use recognised ride-sharing apps or black cabs at night. Watch the sloping cobbles which are slippery when wet and remember traffic drives on the left.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use common urban precautions: avoid poorly lit isolated spots at night, take licensed transport if unsure, wear suitable footwear for cobbles, and be mindful of left-side traffic when crossing roads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility of attractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Most modern hotels and attractions are accessible, but many older buildings (guesthouses, some pubs and restaurants) lack ramps and lifts. The New Town with wide streets is more straightforward for wheelchair users than the steep, cobbled Old Town. VisitScotland provides a guide to accessible accommodation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check accessibility details for specific attractions/accommodation in advance and consult VisitScotland resources. Expect variable accessibility in historic parts of the city.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tap water is drinkable
rubrics_metrics.description: Edinburgh tap water is safe to drink. You can request tap water for free with a meal in a restaurant. The region’s water is soft (low in dissolved minerals), giving it a fresher taste than water from much of the UK.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring a refillable bottle and drink tap water confidently. If you prefer bottled water, note the soft taste of local tap water.
